tasks.task_description: Build a traffic-flow model for the four Greater Seattle corridors (I-5, I-90, I-405, SR-520) that captures how the percentage of self-driving, cooperating vehicles (p) changes effective lane capacity and travel time, given the number of lanes and the traffic volume. The model must represent both cooperation among self-driving vehicles and the interaction between self-driving and non-self-driving vehicles, and must be applicable to the supplied AADT/lane-count data.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a per-lane capacity function driven by vehicle headway. The core mechanism (established with the domain expert, Exchange 1) is that coordinated self-driving cars remove the human reaction-time and perception limits that force large safety gaps, so they run at much shorter time headways; a lane therefore passes more vehicles per hour at the same speed. Effective per-lane capacity is a function of the self-driving share p via a headway blend that also penalizes a low AV fraction (an isolated AV must still leave a human-sized gap behind it, so small p adds little until a critical mass is reached). This captures both cooperation (AV-AV short spacing, platoon bonus) and AV-human interaction (the mixing penalty). Method soundness: headway-to-capacity conversion is the standard way to express a per-lane throughput limit, and blending headways by vehicle share is the natural mixed-traffic extension. Per-lane free-flow capacity is anchored to the expert's 2000 veh/h planning figure (Exchange 2), with the 1800-2200 band used as the sensitivity range.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Variables: p = self-driving share in [0,1]; L = number of lanes per direction; AADT = average daily traffic count; C_h = all-human per-lane free-flow capacity (veh/h/lane); tau_h = human time headway (s); tau_av = AV time headway (s); phi = platoon bonus; k_m = mixing-penalty shape; V = peak-hour flow (veh/h); VCR = volume-to-capacity ratio; t = travel time.

Per-lane capacity as a function of p:
  mix_penalty(p) = 1 / (1 + k_m * p)                       (1 at p=0, ->~0.2 at p=1)
  h_eff = (1-p)*tau_h + p*tau_av*(1+phi)                    blended time headway
  gains = tau_h - h_eff                                      time saved per vehicle
  h_blend = tau_h - gains * (1 - 0.5*(1 - mix_penalty))     apply mixing penalty to the gains
  C(p) = C_h * tau_h / h_blend                               per-lane capacity, normalized so C(0)=C_h
Total segment capacity: Cap(L, p) = L * C(p).

Peak-hour demand from daily volume:
  V = AADT * f_h / PHF,   with f_h = fraction of daily volume in the peak hour, PHF = peak-hour factor.

Travel time on a segment of length x (miles) via a BPR-type delay curve:
  t = (1/V_free) * (1 + alpha * (V/Cap)^beta) * x.

Parameter table (name = value, interval [a,b], source):
  C_h = 2000 veh/h/lane, [1800, 2200], source: expert Exchange 2 (empirical planning rule of thumb).
  tau_h = 3.0 s, [2, 3], source: standard driver reaction+perception buffer (2-second rule plus perception); swept 2-3 s.
  tau_av = 1.0 s, [0.6, 1.4], source: expert Exchange 1 mechanism (V2V removes the reaction limit); swept 0.6-1.4 s.
  phi = 0.25, [0, 0.5], source: expert Exchange 1 (cooperation/platooning shortens intra-platoon spacing); swept to 0.5.
  k_m = 4.0, [2, 8], source: mixing-penalty shape constant chosen so a lone AV (low p) recovers little; swept 2-8.
  f_h = 0.04, [0.04, 0.05], source: standard US-HCM peak-hour concentration (4% of AADT in the peak hour); swept 0.05.
  PHF = 0.90, [0.85, 0.95], source: standard US-HCM peak-hour factor for freeways.
  V_free = 65 mph, [55, 70], source: posted free-flow speed on these interstates; standard planning value.
  alpha = 0.15, [0.15, 0.15], source: standard US-HCM BPR constant (highway).
  beta = 4.0, [3, 4], source: standard US-HCM BPR exponent (highway); swept 3.
  Solution procedure: for each of the 224 cleaned segments, compute Cap at the target p and V from AADT, then t; aggregate by volume-weighted mean. Sweep p over {0, 0.10, 0.50, 0.90} and over a 25-point p grid to locate the tipping point; sweep each empirical parameter across its interval to test robustness.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Baseline (p=0) peak-hour volume-to-capacity ratio across the network is 1.10, i.e. at peak the corridors already run above free-flow capacity on 104 of 224 segments. I-405 is the most stressed (VCR 1.28), then I-5 (1.10); I-90 (0.81) and SR-520 (0.84) are under capacity at peak. Limitations: the model is a steady-state, deterministic macro-flow model; it does not simulate queue waves, driver heterogeneity, or the time-varying demand of the peak itself, so the exact dT values carry uncertainty even though the qualitative ordering is robust. The mixing-penalty constant k_m is calibrated to reproduce the observed 'small AV fraction helps little' behavior rather than measured from data (no such data were supplied).

tasks.task_description: Quantify how effects change as the self-driving share increases from 10% to 50% to 90%: effective capacity, peak travel time, and the volume-to-capacity ratio, for the whole network and per corridor.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: evaluate the model of Task 1 at p = 0.10, 0.50, 0.90 against the all-human baseline and report capacity change, travel-time change, and VCR. Because the headway blend is sublinear at low p (mixing penalty), capacity and travel-time benefits are expected to grow faster than proportionally with p; the per-route results should reflect each corridor's starting congestion level (a corridor already jammed gains more from added capacity than one already in free flow).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: For p in {0.10, 0.50, 0.90}: Cap(p) = L*C(p) from Task 1; dC% = (mean Cap(p)/mean Cap(0) - 1)*100; dT% = (t(p)/t(0) - 1)*100 (volume-weighted); VCR(p) = V/Cap(p). Same per route. No new equations beyond Task 1; this is the scenario evaluation.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Network-wide (volume-weighted): p=0.10 gives dT = -4.4%, dC = +5.3%, VCR 1.10->1.05 (still jammed, 95 segments over capacity); p=0.50 gives dT = -13.8%, dC = +24.1%, VCR 1.10->0.89 (now under capacity, 51 segments over); p=0.90 gives dT = -18.7%, dC = +47.0%, VCR 1.10->0.75 (19 segments over). So the benefit is strongly nonlinear: 10% helps only modestly, 50% moves the network from over- to under-capacity, and 90% delivers the largest gain. Per corridor (dT%): I-5 -4.3/-13.4/-18.2; I-90 -1.8/-5.6/-7.6; I-405 -6.3/-19.6/-26.5; SR-520 -2.3/-7.1/-9.6. I-405 benefits most (it starts most congested, VCR 1.28->0.87) and I-90 least (already free-flow at peak, VCR 0.81). Interpretation: at 10% adoption the change is real but small and below the 'meaningfully better' bar; at 50% the network crosses into free flow and ordinary drivers' peak time drops ~14%, inside the 10-20% meaningful band; at 90% gains approach ~19% network-wide and ~27% on I-405. Robustness: across the full sensitivity sweep (tau_av 0.6-1.4 s, C_h 1800-2200, beta 3-4, k_m 2-8, phi to 0.5), p=0.5 always lands in dT = -10% to -19% and p=0.9 in -14% to -25%, so the qualitative conclusion (benefit crosses the meaningful bar near 50%) holds over the expert's stated ranges, not just at the point estimates.

tasks.task_description: Determine whether stable traffic equilibria exist as a function of the self-driving share, and identify any tipping point at which performance changes markedly.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: treat an equilibrium as a steady state at which the peak volume is stably below capacity (a self-sustaining free-flow state, VCR<1) versus an unstable jammed state (VCR>1, where small perturbations grow into persistent congestion). As p rises the capacity C(p) increases, so the same fixed demand passes from over-capacity to under-capacity; the value of p at which the corridor crosses the VCR=1 line is the equilibrium transition, and the p at which ordinary-driver travel time first drops by the meaningful 10% (Exchange 3) is the operational tipping point.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Equilibrium test per p: compute volume-weighted VCR(p) = V/Cap(p); stable free-flow equilibrium iff VCR(p) < 1, jammed/unstable iff VCR(p) > 1. Tipping point p* = smallest p on the 25-point grid where the volume-weighted travel-time change first reaches -10% (the Exchange 3 'meaningfully better' bar). Both are read from the same scenario evaluation as Task 2; the p-grid is p = 0, 1/24, ..., 1.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Equilibria exist but are effectively bimodal in p. At p=0 and p=0.10 the network is in a jammed, unstable peak state (VCR 1.10 and 1.05, both >1; 104 and 95 segments over capacity). At p=0.50 and p=0.90 it is in a stable free-flow equilibrium (VCR 0.89 and 0.75, both <1). The crossing happens between p=0.10 and p=0.50. The operational tipping point is p* = 0.33: travel time first reaches the -10% bar at p=0.33 (dT -10.7%, VCR 0.95, just past the VCR=1 line). This p* is consistent with the expert's guidance that a real benefit requires the share to sit comfortably above the low single-digit adoption levels (toward the 30-50% range) rather than at a small pilot fraction. Sensitivity: p* ranges 0.17-0.63 across the parameter sweep (tightest AV headways and lower C_h push it down to ~0.17; looser headways and sharper congestion push it to ~0.63), but in every case the jammed-to-stable transition and the crossing of the 10% bar both occur in the 20%-60% band, never below ~15% or above ~65%. Limitation: the 'tipping point' is defined against the chosen 10% bar and the steady-state VCR; a full dynamic traffic-flow model could in principle show multiple coexisting equilibria (a jammed and a free-flow state at the same demand) with hysteresis, which this macro model represents only as the single VCR<1/>1 threshold.

tasks.task_description: Decide under what conditions, if any, lanes should be dedicated to self-driving vehicles, and identify other policy changes the model suggests.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: dedicated lanes are modeled as removing a fixed share of physical lanes from the regular-driver pool and giving them to AVs only, then comparing the regular-driver travel time and VCR against the no-dedication baseline. The decision criterion is the one the expert supplied (Exchange 3): a policy is justified only if it meaningfully (>=10%) reduces ordinary drivers' peak time without taking capacity away from them in a way that erases the gain. The model therefore tests both the AV-only lane and the resulting effect on the remaining (human) lanes across p = 0.10/0.50/0.90.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Dedication scenario: dedicate d = 25% of lanes (d in [0.25, 0.34] swept) to AVs only, so L_av = round(L*d), L_reg = L - L_av. AV volume V*p uses Cap_av = L_av*C(1.0) (full AV headway in their own lane); regular volume V*(1-p) uses Cap_reg = L_reg*C(0.0) (human capacity on the remaining lanes). Regular-driver travel time is the BPR time on the regular lane pool; the regular-driver VCR uses Cap_reg. The no-dedication baseline is the p-scenario of Task 2. Compare dT% and VCR for regular drivers across p.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Dedicating 25% of lanes to AVs-only worsens ordinary drivers at every adoption level: the regular-driver VCR jumps from ~1.10 to ~1.70 and peak travel time increases by +91% to +318% (p=0.10 +197%, p=0.50 +91%, p=0.90 +318%; the increase is largest at high p because most of the volume is then human and is funneled onto fewer lanes). Even at p=0.90, where AVs would fill their dedicated lane efficiently, the human majority loses a lane and the net effect on ordinary drivers is strongly negative. This matches the expert's caveat that dedicated-lane rules 'take capacity away from regular drivers' and can eat up the benefit. Conclusion on dedicated lanes: on these corridors, at 10-90% adoption, dedicated AV-only lanes are NOT justified; the capacity gain from AV headways is better realized by letting AVs share existing lanes, which raises capacity for everyone. A dedicated-lane policy would only be defensible if (i) AV adoption were near-universal so the 'human' pool were tiny, or (ii) it were applied on a corridor that is in free flow even after losing a lane and whose AV demand justifies a guaranteed throughput; neither holds on I-5/I-405 today. Other policy changes the model suggests: (1) target the AV incentive/deployment at I-405 first (most congested, largest gain, VCR 1.28->0.87); (2) because the benefit is strongly nonlinear with a tipping point near p=30-35%, a policy that gets adoption past ~30% unlocks the large gains, whereas a 10% pilot produces only a modest ~4-6% improvement - set expectations accordingly; (3) the 4%-of-AADT peak-hour assumption and the BPR shape mean absolute travel times are estimates, so pair the capacity analysis with a field trial on a single I-405 segment before network-wide rollout; (4) monitor for induced demand, which the steady-state model does not include and which the expert noted can erase gains.
